lookForward.fits: Fat Bear Week 2026 at Katmai National Park, voting 22 to 29 September, champion crowned Tuesday.
lookForward.headline: Fat Bear Week: vote for a bear by Tuesday
lookForward.line: In Katmai National Park, Alaska, the brown bears have spent the summer eating salmon and are now magnificently round. The park runs a knockout bracket and the public picks the fattest, free, once a day at fatbearweek.org. Champion crowned Tuesday.

source.name: National Park Service: Fat Bear Week 2026

more: Katmai National Park is on the Alaska Peninsula, a place with more brown bears than people. In late summer the bears stand in the Brooks River and catch sockeye salmon as the fish leap the falls, eating as much as they can before winter. A bear that goes into its den in October will not eat again until spring, so the fatter, the better.

Fat Bear Week turns that into a game. The park picks twelve or so bears, shows a photo of each from July and one from September, and pairs them in a knockout bracket. Anyone can vote once a day at fatbearweek.org, free, no account needed. Voting runs from Tuesday 22 September to Tuesday 29 September 2026, when the champion is named. Nobody tells the bear.
The live cameras at explore.org show the Brooks Falls all day. Watch for a while; it is very calming, and the salmon are still running.

funFact.statement: A Katmai bear can eat 40 salmon in a day.
funFact.reveal: A big male at Brooks Falls eats dozens a day at the peak. By winter he may weigh a thousand pounds. Then he sleeps.

calmRead.fits: Expands today's look-forward: Fat Bear Week at Katmai.
calmRead.title: The most honest contest in America
calmRead.teaser: Every autumn, Alaska's bears compete for a title they know nothing about.
paragraphs: On a river in southern Alaska, brown bears stand at the top of a small waterfall and catch salmon in their mouths as the fish leap upstream. They have done this for thousands of years. Since 2014, a webcam has watched them, and once a year the internet votes on which bear has got fattest. This is Fat Bear Week, and it is the best thing the National Park Service does.

The fat is not vanity. A Katmai bear must put on enough weight between June and October to sleep through an Alaskan winter without eating or drinking. A big male can go into his den at over a thousand pounds and come out in spring a third lighter. Fat is survival, and the fattest bear is the one who has done the year's work best.

So every September, Katmai's rangers pick a dozen bears, post before-and-after photos, and the public votes in a bracket, two bears at a time, until one is crowned on the last Tuesday of the month. Voters argue about the bears by number and nickname. Past champions have included a bear called Otis, who won four times by doing almost nothing but sitting in the best spot, and a mother bear called Grazer who beat the biggest male in the river.
The bears are unaware of all this. They keep fishing. That is the point of it, really: a contest with no losers, judged by strangers, where the prize is winter.

source.name: National Park Service: Fat Bear Week 2026

word.fits: The first cool rain of the fall.
word.meaning: The smell of rain on dry ground. Coined in 1964 from the Greek for stone and for the blood of the gods. Fall's first cold front brings it.

kindness.text: Leave the last flowers in your garden standing this week. A monarch on its way to Mexico needs the fuel.

joke.setup: How does a Katmai bear prepare for winter?
joke.punchline: Salmon, salmon, salmon, nap. Same as a Sunday, only longer.

riddle.riddle: I win by eating, I lose nothing, and I sleep through the celebration. What am I?
